about.title: About Datawriter, By CUAI
about.heading: Datawriter
about.org_body: , the Columbia University chapter of Amnesty International. Datawriter is a free browser extension built by student volunteers. It is not affiliated with trackdatacenters.com, whose public data it reads, or with any government body it lists, and it does not speak for Amnesty International as a whole.
about.p_purpose: Large data centers are approved by local boards, often with little notice and under code names. Datawriter turns a ZIP code into the nearest tracked project, puts its size in everyday terms, names the officials who will decide, and writes a letter to each of them that opens in your own email. It saves the hours it takes to find the right official, the right facts and the right words.
about.step1: Type your ZIP or town. Datawriter finds the nearest data center project on the tracker.
about.step2: See who decides: the local, county and state officials, with their published contacts.
about.step3: Press the envelope button beside an official, or the green bar under the project title. A letter opens in your email, already filled in. You press Send.
about.src_projects: Projects, sizes and stages: {link}, read live on its own pages.
about.src_officials: Officials, titles, emails and portraits: the governments' own websites, collected in October 2026 and dated in each record. Names found only in search results are left out. Where a 2026 name or title could not be confirmed, the panel says so. Party labels appear only where a source states them.
about.src_comparisons: Comparisons: EIA, the Census Bureau, NEA, NCES, USDA, EPA, AHA and others, listed in full in the project's source list (docs/sources.md).
about.src_zip: ZIP code locations: GeoNames (CC BY 4.0). Satellite imagery: Esri.
about.p_privacy: Datawriter sends nothing on its own. Your name, address, email and phone stay in your browser's local storage and appear only in letters you choose to send. The only outside services it contacts are the tracker, Esri's map service for pictures, and a public ZIP lookup for ZIP codes outside the bundled states.
about.dd_coverage: 31 states and the District of Columbia
about.p_feedback: Found a wrong name or a dead link? Check the official site linked on the card, then tell CU Amnesty International so the next release can fix it.
about.footer: Datawriter, By CUAI · Created by CU Amnesty International (CUAI), the Columbia University chapter of Amnesty International · Free to use and share.
finder.stage_proposed_short: Decision pending: this is when letters matter most.
finder.stage_proposed_note: An application is in front of the planning board, zoning board or council, and the votes are still ahead. Hearings are open to the public, and officials often count the letters they get.
finder.stage_preliminary_short: Early: no application has been filed yet.
finder.stage_preliminary_note: Land deals, utility requests or news reports, but no application yet. Letters now can shape the rules: ask for a moratorium, a data center ordinance and disclosure requirements.
finder.stage_delayed_short: Stalled: public pressure can shape whether it comes back.
finder.stage_delayed_note: The project is paused or has missed its schedule. Letters asking officials to let approvals lapse, or to add conditions before any restart, carry weight.
finder.stage_expansion_short: An expansion usually needs new approvals.
finder.stage_expansion_note: The first phase exists, but an expansion usually goes back to the same boards for approval. Letters can win conditions on power, water and noise that the first phase may have lacked.
finder.stage_construction_note: Zoning is usually settled. Letters still count for air and water permits, noise and lighting conditions, tax deals and any future phases.
finder.stage_operational_note: The site exists. Letters matter for enforcement: electricity rates, water use, noise complaints and the next expansion request.
finder.stage_withdrawn_short: Pulled by the developer, but it could return.
finder.stage_withdrawn_note: Withdrawn applications are often refiled. Letters asking for a moratorium or a stricter ordinance make it harder for the project to come back on the same terms.
finder.stage_rejected_note: Send a thank-you note and press for a permanent ordinance. Watch for an appeal or a revised application, which would reopen the window.
finder.stage_retired_note: No decision is pending. Letters matter only if the site is proposed for reuse.
finder.stage_unrecorded_short: Stage not recorded by the tracker.
finder.stage_unknown_note: Check the project page for its current status before writing.

letter.tone_questions_short: Asks for written answers before any vote
letter.tone_conditions_short: Approve only with binding protections in writing
letter.detail_brief_short: Power and water, and the first three asks
letter.detail_standard_short: Adds noise, land and jobs, and a fourth ask where there is one
letter.ask_moratorium: Support a moratorium on new approvals until an independent, public study of the impact on electricity rates, water supply, and local budgets is complete.
letter.ask_require_full_cost: Require, for this and any future project, that the developer pay the full cost of grid and water infrastructure, publicly disclose energy and water use, meet enforceable noise and air standards, and face residents at a public hearing before any vote.
letter.ask_federal: Use your office to call on state and federal lawmakers to slow the pace of AI infrastructure buildout until enforceable safety standards, independent oversight, and public accountability for these systems are in place.
letter.ask_unless: unless {dev} first pays the full cost of the grid and water infrastructure it uses, discloses its energy and water use publicly, and meets enforceable noise and air standards
letter.ask_utility_pay: Require data center developers to pay the full cost of the transmission and substation upgrades they trigger, and reject any rate design that shifts those costs onto households and small businesses.
letter.ask_utility_interconnection: Make interconnection requests for projects like {project} public, with their expected load, before they are approved.
letter.ask_env_permits: Scrutinize every air, water and stormwater permit sought for {project}, require public disclosure of its water use and generator emissions, and deny permits that cannot meet enforceable standards.
letter.ask_commerce_withhold: Withhold state incentives, tax abatements and site-readiness grants from {project} and from any data center that will not pay its full infrastructure costs and employ a meaningful permanent workforce.
letter.ask_commerce_publish: Publish the full cost to taxpayers of every incentive already offered to data center developers in our state.
letter.ask_state_moratorium: Support a statewide moratorium on new data center approvals until an independent, public study of the impact on electricity rates, water supply, and local budgets is complete.
letter.ask_state_direct_agencies: Direct state agencies to require that developers of projects like {project} pay the full cost of grid and water infrastructure, publicly disclose energy and water use, and meet enforceable noise and air standards.
letter.ask_state_federal: Use your office to call on federal lawmakers to slow the pace of AI infrastructure buildout until enforceable safety standards, independent oversight, and public accountability for these systems are in place.
letter.ask_planning_late: Recommend against any expansion, variance or new site plan for {project} {unless}.
letter.ask_planning: Recommend denial of the rezoning, land development plan or special use permit for {project} when it comes before you, and recommend against any future data center proposal in our jurisdiction.
letter.ask_zoning: Deny any variance, special exception or conditional use sought for {project}{expansion}, and hold {dev} to every standard in our ordinance.
letter.ask_staff: Make every application, study and agreement connected to {project} public as soon as it is filed, and give residents real notice and a real hearing before any decision.
letter.ask_governing_late: Oppose any further rezoning, expansion, permit or incentive for {project} {unless}, and oppose any new data center proposal in our jurisdiction on the same terms.
letter.ask_governing: Vote against the rezoning, special use permit or incentive package for {project} when it comes before you{onDate}, and against any future data center proposal in our jurisdiction.
letter.q_who_pays: Who will pay for the transmission, substation and water upgrades that {project} requires: {dev}, or every household on the system?
letter.q_water: How much water will its cooling consume each day, from what source, and who will verify it?
letter.q_noise_gens: What noise, air and lighting standards will apply to its {gens} diesel backup generators and its round-the-clock equipment, and who will enforce them?
letter.q_noise: What noise, air and lighting standards will apply to its backup generators and its round-the-clock equipment, and who will enforce them?
letter.q_abatements: Which tax abatements or incentives are being requested, for how many years, and what will our schools, roads and emergency services forgo?
letter.q_state_incentives: Which state incentives, grants or tax exemptions does {project} qualify for, and what will they cost taxpayers over their term?
letter.q_jobs: How many permanent jobs are guaranteed in writing, and what happens if they do not materialize?
letter.q_hearing: When is the public hearing, how will residents be notified, and will the full application be public before it?
letter.c_full_cost: {dev} pays the full cost of every grid, substation and water upgrade the project triggers, with no cost shifted to ratepayers.
letter.c_disclosure: Energy and water use are disclosed publicly every year, with independent verification.
letter.c_limits: Enforceable noise, air and lighting limits are written into the approval, with penalties and the power to revoke it.
letter.c_jobs: No tax abatement or incentive is granted unless the permanent jobs promised are guaranteed in writing and clawed back if they do not materialize.
letter.c_bond: A decommissioning bond covers the cost of removing the facility if it closes.
letter.c_hearing: Residents get a public hearing on the full application, with real notice, before any vote.

letter.to_officials_copied: To the officials copied on this message:
letter.stand_vote: how you intend to vote on {project}
letter.rights: Every community has a right to clean water, breathable air, and affordable energy.
letter.closing_oppose: The people you represent should not subsidize some of the most profitable corporations in the world, or absorb the risks of a race they were never asked to join. Thank you for your attention to this urgent matter. I look forward to your response and to learning {stand}.
letter.p1_oppose: {rights} This project puts all three at risk. {power} {water} {noise}
letter.p2_oppose: These costs fall on residents. The benefits do not. {benefits}
letter.p3_oppose: Supporters will say this project brings jobs and tax revenue, and that if we refuse it, it will simply be built somewhere else. {promised} The tax revenue is what remains after the abatements the developer demands as a condition of coming here. And a project that only makes sense when a community absorbs its costs is not one we are obligated to accept.
letter.p4_oppose: There is a larger reason for caution. Facilities like {project} are the physical footprint of an artificial intelligence buildout moving faster than any safeguard around it. The companies racing to build these systems have themselves warned of serious risks, from mass displacement of workers to misuse by bad actors, yet no binding safety standards govern how these systems are developed or deployed. Local governments are being asked to lock in decades of land, water, and grid capacity for a technology whose protections do not yet exist. Communities have every right to say: not at this speed, and not without accountability.
letter.closing_questions: Residents have a right to know, before a decision is taken, what this project will cost them and who will bear it. I would appreciate written answers before any {vote}, and I will share them with my neighbors. Thank you for your time. I look forward to your response.
letter.promises_not_commitments: Residents are being asked to accept these costs on the strength of promises, not commitments.
letter.intro_conditions_planning: The conditions, which any recommendation to approve should carry:
letter.closing_conditions: Every community has a right to clean water, breathable air, and affordable energy, and an approval that does not protect them in writing does not protect them at all. A project that cannot meet these conditions is not one our community can afford. Thank you for your attention. I look forward to your response and to learning which of these you will insist on.
letter.subject_oppose_late: {project}{inTown}: please hold it to enforceable conditions
letter.call_ask_oppose_late: I'm asking {official} to hold it to enforceable conditions, and to make sure the developer pays its own grid and water costs.
letter.call_ask_oppose: I'm asking {official} to oppose it, and to make sure the developer pays its own grid and water costs.
letter.call_ask_questions: I'd like to know, before any {vote}, who pays for the grid upgrades and what noise and air limits will apply, and I'd like that answered in writing.
letter.call_ask_conditions: I'm asking that it be approved only if the developer pays its own grid and water costs, discloses its energy and water use, and meets enforceable noise and air limits.

popup.home_five_digits: Enter all five digits of your home ZIP.
letter.ask_planning_past: Recommend denial of any revived or successor application for {project}, and recommend against any future data center proposal in our jurisdiction.
letter.ask_governing_past: Oppose any revived or successor application for {project}, and vote against any future data center proposal in our jurisdiction.
letter.q_hearing_past: If this project or a successor is refiled, will residents get a public hearing on the full application, with real notice, before any vote?
letter.opening_questions_past: I am writing {who} about {about}. Should this project or a successor return, I am asking you to obtain written answers to the questions below before any decision is made, and to make them public.
letter.opening_conditions_past: I am writing {who} about {about}. Should this project or a successor return, I ask that any approval carry the binding conditions below.
letter.closing_questions_past: Residents have a right to know, before a decision is taken, what a project like this would cost them and who will bear it. I would appreciate written answers before any future vote, and I will share them with my neighbors. Thank you for your time. I look forward to your response.
panel.carbon_cars: About what {cars} gasoline cars put out in a year
panel.carbon_grid_note: Running flat out on the {state} grid at its {year} average emission rate (EIA State Electricity Profiles). Cleaner or dirtier supply changes the figure.
panel.carbon_gas_note: Running flat out on its own natural gas plant, at the emission standard for a new combined-cycle gas turbine (EPA, 800 lb CO2 per MWh).
panel.jobs_per_acre: One permanent job for every {acres} acres
panel.jobs_construction_line: Plus {n} construction jobs while it is built
panel.jobs_note: Jobs as reported by the developer or in public records; permanent counts are rarely guaranteed in writing.
panel.timeline_note: The zoning and permit decisions come early in this span; by the opening date they are long settled.
panel.dyk_depreciation: The computers inside a data center are written off in about five years. Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta depreciate their servers over five to six years, and AI chips turn over faster still. A fifteen-year tax abatement outlasts the equipment two or three times over.
panel.dyk_jobs: Across the projects on this tracker that report jobs, the typical data center promises {perm} permanent jobs and {build} construction jobs. The construction jobs end when the building does.
panel.dyk_power: Data centers used about 4.4 percent of all U.S. electricity in 2023 and could use between 6.7 and 12 percent by 2028, according to the Department of Energy's 2024 report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.
